Female Daubed shanny attain a maximum total length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters], a value that distinguishes them from several smaller-bodied congeners in the Arctic ichthyofauna. In this species, the total length at which females first become capable of reproduction, known as length at puberty, has been recorded at 12.5 centimeters [Lp = 12.5 centimeters], marking a distinct size threshold for the onset of gonadal maturation. Field surveys conducted in the Barents Sea indicate that individuals achieving this length reliably exhibit developing oocytes, confirming the transition from the immature juvenile phase to a reproductively viable state. The relationship between length and fecundity is tightly coupled in this species, and the attainment of a moderate body size prior to reproductive effort is thought to reflect an adaptive strategy to balance somatic growth against the energetic demands of gamete production under the cold, resource-limited conditions of polar waters.

At the time of eclosion, newly emerged yolk-sac larvae possess a minute wet weight at birth of just 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter documented in related stichaeid species. This initial mass is drawn almost entirely from the endogenous yolk reserves of the fertilised ovum, which must sustain the endotrophic larva through the critical period before the onset of exogenous feeding. The chorionase-driven hatching event marks the beginning of a lecithotrophic phase during which the prolarva relies entirely on its yolk sac for metabolic fuel. Rapid yolk absorption is essential, as the window for first prey capture is narrow; failure to commence active feeding before the depletion of these reserves leads to the point of no return. The modest birth mass underscores the high fecundity necessary to offset the considerable mortality typical of early planktonic life stages in the Arctic ecosystem.

Field studies under controlled conditions have documented a daily reproduction rate at the standard body length of 11 centimeters, calculated as approximately 7.65 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 7.65 offspring per year] when maintained at a water temperature of 2.3 °C [T = 2.3 °C]. This reproductive output reflects the combined product of clutch size and spawning frequency for individuals that have not yet reached their ultimate length. The temperature dependence of this parameter is pronounced, as metabolic processes governing vitellogenesis and oocyte maturation are tightly constrained by ambient thermal regimes. At the cooler end of the species' thermal range, reproductive rates decline measurably, suggesting that the 2.3 °C [T = 2.3 °C] benchmark represents a near-optimal thermal window for reproductive investment in this Arctic-adapted fish. The observed rate of approximately 7.65 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 7.65 offspring per year] at 11 centimeters total length provides a key parameter for estimating population-level recruitment in dynamic polar environments.

The ultimate female wet weight, representing the asymptotic body mass achieved by fully grown adults, is approximately 24.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 24.4 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions for this species. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty, the mass at which females first exhibit gonadal recrudescence and become capable of spawning, is considerably lower at approximately 6.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 6.1 grams]. This nearly four-fold difference in mass between the pubertal and ultimate stages indicates that a substantial portion of somatic growth occurs after the onset of reproductive capability. Such a pattern is typical of fish species that exhibit indeterminate growth, where energy allocation shifts gradually from exclusive somatic investment to a mixed strategy encompassing both growth and reproduction. The mass at first spawning is therefore not an indicator of final size, but rather a developmental landmark that permits the individual to begin contributing to the next generation while continuing its own trajectory towards the adult asymptotic mass.

Longevity records for the Daubed shanny, based on comparative data from the closely related Arctic stichaeid Stichaeus punctatus, suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years] at the same thermal regime of 2.3 °C [T = 2.3 °C]. This extended lifespan, spanning over six thousand days, is among the longest documented for small-bodied benthic fish in high-latitude ecosystems and reflects the profoundly slowed metabolic pace enforced by persistent cold temperatures. The life history strategy that emerges from these combined parameters — a moderate size at puberty, a substantial post-pubertal growth trajectory, a modest but sustained daily reproductive output, and an exceptionally long reproductive lifespan — positions the Daubed shanny as an archetypal slow-living, iteroparous Arctic teleost. Such extended longevity allows for multiple reproductive bouts across a lifetime, buffering the species against the stochastic recruitment failures common in polar environments where suitable spawning conditions may not occur annually.
